summary:
G-NOSIS is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12 where the player commands a lunar base for 14 days until the relief crew arrives. To survive, they balance four linked resources: energy, food, health and radiation. Each day brings a real lunar challenge: solar storms, moonquakes, micrometeorites, dust on the solar panels, water leaks and the freezing 14-day lunar night.

The science is the game’s rules. Children predict what will happen, find the evidence in a report, act and see the result. Live NASA data (DONKI space weather, CRaTER radiation from LRO and OSDR plant studies) turn real data into decisions inside the game.

The difficulty adapts to each child without them ever seeing a level. The game includes a narrator, plays in Spanish and English, and offers optional student accounts that use only an alias, so teachers can follow each student’s progress in class.
details:
G-NOSIS: Lunar Base Survival for Young Explorers

What it does and how it works
G-NOSIS is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12. The player is the captain of a lunar base and has to keep it running for 14 days until the relief crew arrives. The base depends on four bars that are always linked: energy, food, health and radiation. Every decision changes all four. Growing food uses energy today and pays off days later. Turning off the heating saves power, but at about −133 °C during the lunar night it hurts the crew’s health. Going to the shelter during a solar storm protects the captain, but sealing the hatches costs energy.

Each day brings an event based on real lunar conditions: solar storms, moonquakes, micrometeorite showers, dust on the panels, water leaks, ice hunting in permanently shadowed craters, and the 14-day lunar night. Events become short minigames. Mission Control calls follow a scientific loop: predict which bar will change, find the sentence in the report that proves it, act, and see the result. Breakdowns are solved by reading clues, some of them misleading, and telling the cause apart from the symptom. Every report goes into a logbook with a dictionary of difficult words. At the end, the player writes a “manual” for the next captain, and the cards matched correctly carry over into the next mission.

Benefits and intended impact
The goal is for children to learn space science by using it, not by memorizing it. The concepts are the rules of the game: the Moon has no global magnetic field or thick atmosphere, solar particles can arrive in less than an hour, the Space Station recycles about 98% of its water, and moon dust is sharp like glass. The game measures understanding through what the child does: whether they predicted correctly, whether they diagnosed a breakdown on the first try, and whether they kept knowledge from earlier missions. In school use, a teacher creates a class with a code, accepts the students and sees which topics are hardest for the group. We want G-NOSIS to work as a classroom tool, especially in Spanish-speaking communities, that turns reading comprehension and scientific reasoning into an adventure.

Tools, languages and software

  • HTML5 Canvas and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks. The Moon and the base are drawn in ASCII and pixel art at 2560×1440.
    • DONKI (solar flares, CMEs and geomagnetic storms) for the space-weather forecast and surprise storms.
    • RadLab / CRaTER (LRO) for a real lunar radiation chart that children read.
    • OSDR for real plant-biology studies in the greenhouse reports.
  • A science-question bank where every fact cites a NASA source and URL. Questions rotate deterministically between missions.
  • Supabase (PostgreSQL with row-level security, plus Auth) for student accounts with an alias only (no email, no real name), class codes and the teacher view.
  • The Web Speech API for a built-in narrator in Spanish and English, which matters for early readers.
  • Python (Pygame and Pillow) for prototypes and animated minigame demos; Node.js for automated tests and a difficulty simulator.
  • Claude Code (Anthropic) as an AI programming assistant.
  • No special hardware: it runs in any modern browser, on a laptop, a tablet or a phone in landscape.

How it is creative
Instead of a quiz with a space theme, G-NOSIS makes science the game’s physics: if you don’t understand the lunar night, you run out of power. The difficulty adapts to each child with two hidden knobs, one for challenge and one for reading, and the child never sees a level. Higher levels include “transfer” questions: the text gives the rule and the question presents a new situation where you have to apply it, so the answer can’t be copied. A friendly guide, Laika, introduces the base, and the colors of the dialog boxes change with the tension of each event. The endings are animated cinematics, so failing becomes a lesson about what went wrong rather than a game-over screen.

Factors we considered

  • Age: short sentences, clear vocabulary, a narrator, large text and a dictionary for young readers.
  • Scientific accuracy: every fact is checked against NASA sources; anything we couldn’t verify is marked and kept out of the question bank.
  • Child privacy: no email or real name, a privacy notice, the option to delete the account, and teacher access only after accepting the student.
  • Accessibility: bilingual, fully playable by mouse, touch or keyboard, and a pause menu to control volume, the narrator, text size and full screen.
  • Fairness: a wrong answer gives a hint and a second try, and children who are struggling get extra support without being labeled.
  • Evidence: a difficulty simulator and automated tests check that the mission can be won and lost, and that no question breaks.
